question: Shri Pramod Sawant took the oath as the Chief Minister of which state in March 2022?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Goa.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Pramod Sawant (BJP) was sworn in as the Chief Minister of Goa for a second term on 28 March 2022, after the BJP won 20 of the 40 seats in the February 2022 Assembly election. (गोवा के मुख्यमंत्री)

• He first became Goa's CM in March 2019 following the death of Manohar Parrikar.

• Goa's capital is Panaji; it became the 25th state of India on 30 May 1987 and was liberated from Portuguese rule in 1961 (Operation Vijay).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Maharashtra — Eknath Shinde took oath as Chief Minister on 30 June 2022.

• Gujarat — Bhupendra Patel took oath in September 2021 and again in December 2022.

• Karnataka — Basavaraj Bommai was Chief Minister in March 2022.

NOTE

• Five states went to polls in early 2022: Goa, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab and Manipur.

• Governor of Goa at that time — P. S. Sreedharan Pillai.

question: Which Bill was passed in the Parliament in 2022 to authorise payment certain sums from and out of the Consolidated Fund of India for the services of the financial year 2022-23?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Appropriation Bill.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Appropriation Bill authorises the government to withdraw money from the Consolidated Fund of India to meet the expenditure of a financial year. (विनियोग विधेयक)

• It is introduced under Article 114 of the Constitution; no money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund except under an appropriation made by law.

• It is a Money Bill (Article 110) — introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations within 14 days.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Finance Bill — deals with the government's taxation proposals (imposition, abolition, alteration of taxes), presented with the Budget under Article 117.

• Electricity (Amendment) Bill, 2022 — sought to allow multiple distribution licensees in the same supply area.

• Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Bill, 2022 — implemented India's obligations under CITES.

NOTE

• Budget-related terms: Article 112 — Annual Financial Statement, Article 113 — demands for grants, Article 114 — Appropriation Bill, Article 266 — Consolidated Fund of India.

• Vote on Account allows spending in advance pending passage of the Appropriation Bill.

question: Which article of the Indian constitution provides for proclamation of Emergency?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Article 352.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Article 352 provides for the proclamation of a National Emergency on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion. (राष्ट्रीय आपातकाल)

• The words "armed rebellion" replaced "internal disturbance" by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.

• A National Emergency has been proclaimed three times in India — 1962 (China war), 1971 (Pakistan war) and 1975 (internal disturbance).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Article 350 — right to submit a representation for redress of grievances in any language used in the Union or a State; 350A — mother-tongue instruction at primary stage; 350B — Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.

• Article 362 — dealt with rights and privileges of rulers of Indian States (repealed by the 26th Amendment, 1971).

• Article 364 — special provisions relating to major ports and aerodromes.

NOTE

• Types of Emergency: Article 352 — National, Article 356 — President's Rule (State), Article 360 — Financial Emergency (never used).

• Emergency provisions are in Part XVIII and were borrowed from the Government of India Act, 1935 / Weimar Constitution of Germany.

question: Which activity symbolizes the celebration of Uttarayan festival in Gujarat?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kite Flying.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Uttarayan is the Gujarati name for Makar Sankranti, celebrated on 14 January, and is famous for mass kite flying (पतंग उड़ाना).

• The festival marks the transition of the Sun into Makara (Capricorn) and the beginning of Uttarayan — the northward journey of the Sun.

• The International Kite Festival is held annually at Ahmedabad, Gujarat, drawing kite-flyers from around the world.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Lighting of diyas is associated with Diwali/Deepavali.

• Bursting crackers is also linked mainly with Diwali.

• Gold shopping is customary on Dhanteras and Akshaya Tritiya.

NOTE

• Makar Sankranti's regional names: Pongal (Tamil Nadu), Magh Bihu/Bhogali Bihu (Assam), Lohri (Punjab, a day earlier), Khichdi (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar), Poush Parbon (West Bengal).

• Other Gujarati festivals: Navratri (Garba), Rann Utsav in Kutch, Tarnetar Fair.

question: Which Indian reformer is regarded as the "Father of Bengali Prose"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (1820–1891) is called the "Father of Bengali Prose" for simplifying and modernising Bengali prose writing. (बांग्ला गद्य के जनक)

• His primer 'Barna Parichay' standardised the Bengali alphabet and is still used to teach Bengali.

• He was the moving force behind the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856, and campaigned against polygamy and child marriage; he was Principal of Sanskrit College, Kolkata.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Keshab Chandra Sen — leader of the Brahmo Samaj; founded the Bharatvarshiya Brahmo Samaj and later Sadharan Brahmo Samaj split from him; influenced the Native Marriage Act, 1872.

• Bankim Chandra Chatterjee — author of 'Anandamath', which contains 'Vande Mataram', and of India's first major Bengali novel 'Durgeshnandini'.

• Swami Dayanand Saraswati — founder of the Arya Samaj (1875), gave the slogan "Back to the Vedas" and wrote 'Satyarth Prakash'.

NOTE

• Titles: Raja Ram Mohan Roy — Father of Indian Renaissance; Jyotiba Phule — Mahatma; Vidyasagar — Father of Bengali Prose.

question: As per census 2011, which among the following is the most spoken language of India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hindi.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• As per Census 2011, Hindi is the most spoken language in India, being the mother tongue of about 43.6% of the population (roughly 52.8 crore people). (हिन्दी — सर्वाधिक बोली जाने वाली भाषा)

• The next most spoken languages are Bengali (8.03%), Marathi (6.86%), Telugu (6.70%) and Tamil (5.70%).

• Hindi in Devanagari script is the official language of the Union under Article 343, with English as an associate official language.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Marathi ranked third and Telugu fourth among mother tongues in Census 2011.

• English is not among the top mother tongues of India; very few Indians report it as their mother tongue.

• The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution presently lists 22 languages.

NOTE

• Census 2011 was the 15th national census and the 7th after Independence; its slogan was "Our Census, Our Future".

• Classical languages of India include Tamil (first, 2004), Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Odia.

question: Swami Vivekananda gave his famous speech at the Parliament of World Religions in Chicago in ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1893.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Swami Vivekananda delivered his celebrated address at the Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago, on 11 September 1893, beginning with the words "Sisters and Brothers of America". (शिकागो भाषण — 1893)

• Born Narendranath Datta on 12 January 1863 in Kolkata, he was the chief disciple of Ramakrishna Paramahamsa.

• He founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897 at Belur Math, near Kolkata.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• 1891–1892 were the years of Vivekananda's travels across India as a wandering monk (parivrajaka), including his visit to Kanyakumari in December 1892.

• He passed away on 4 July 1902 at Belur Math at the age of 39.

• His major works include 'Raja Yoga', 'Karma Yoga', 'Jnana Yoga' and 'Bhakti Yoga'.

NOTE

• 12 January, his birth anniversary, is observed as National Youth Day in India (since 1985).

• 11 September is celebrated as World Brotherhood Day commemorating his Chicago speech.

question: Which of the following planets has the shortest rotation period?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jupiter.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Jupiter has the shortest rotation period of all planets in the Solar System — it completes one spin on its axis in about 9 hours 55 minutes. (घूर्णन काल)

• This very fast rotation makes Jupiter noticeably oblate (flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator).

• Jupiter is the largest planet, a gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium, with the Great Red Spot, a giant storm, on its surface.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Venus has the longest rotation period — about 243 Earth days — and rotates clockwise (retrograde), like Uranus.

• Mercury rotates once in about 59 Earth days and has the shortest revolution period (88 days) around the Sun.

• Mars rotates in about 24 hours 37 minutes, very close to Earth's day.

NOTE

• Rotation = spin on axis; Revolution = orbit around the Sun.

• Jupiter's four largest moons — Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto — are called the Galilean moons; Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System.

question: Which among the following is NOT a way to acquire Citizenship of India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is By Renunciation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Under the Citizenship Act, 1955, Indian citizenship can be acquired in five ways: by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and by incorporation of territory. (नागरिकता अर्जन)

• Renunciation is a mode of losing/termination of citizenship, not of acquiring it — a citizen voluntarily gives up Indian citizenship by making a declaration.

• The other two ways of losing citizenship are termination (voluntarily acquiring another country's citizenship) and deprivation (compulsory, by the Government).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• By Birth — persons born in India between 26 January 1950 and 1 July 1987 are citizens by birth (later conditions were tightened).

• By Registration — for persons of Indian origin, spouses of Indian citizens, and OCI cardholders, subject to residence conditions.

• By Naturalisation — for foreigners who fulfil qualifications including a prescribed period of residence in India.

NOTE

• Citizenship provisions are in Part II, Articles 5 to 11 of the Constitution; Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship by law.

• India provides single citizenship for the whole country, borrowed from the British model.

question: Who among the following was daughter of Iltutmish, a ruler of Slave/Mamluk dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Razia Sultan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Razia Sultan (Raziyya al-Din) was the daughter of Shams-ud-din Iltutmish and ruled Delhi from 1236 to 1240 CE. (रजिया सुल्तान)

• She was the first and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate and of medieval Delhi, nominated by Iltutmish himself in preference to his sons.

• She was opposed by the Turkish nobility (the Chahalgani / Group of Forty) and was ultimately deposed and killed in 1240.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Iltutmish (1211–1236) was the real consolidator of the Slave dynasty; he introduced the silver tanka and copper jital, and completed the Qutub Minar.

• Harkha (Harka Bai / Jodha Bai) was a Rajput princess of Amber and wife of Akbar, not related to Iltutmish.

• Kubra Noorzai and Shafiqa Ziayee were 20th-century Afghan women ministers.

NOTE

• Slave/Mamluk dynasty rulers: Qutub-ud-din Aibak (founder, 1206), Aram Shah, Iltutmish, Razia, Balban — ended in 1290 with the rise of the Khaljis.

• Qutub-ud-din Aibak built the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque (Delhi) and Adhai Din ka Jhonpra (Ajmer).

question: Pandit Birju Maharaj choreographed the song 'Kahe Chhed Mohe' from the movie Devdas. He was mainly associated with which dance form?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kathak.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Pandit Birju Maharaj (1938–2022) was the foremost exponent of the Kathak dance form and belonged to the Lucknow 'Kalka-Bindadin' gharana. (कथक)

• He choreographed 'Kahe Chhed Mohe' in *Devdas* (2002) and also worked in films such as 'Umrao Jaan', 'Dedh Ishqiya' and 'Bajirao Mastani'.

• He was awarded the Padma Vibhushan (1986), the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award and a National Film Award for Best Choreography (2012, for 'Vishwaroopam').

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Bharatanatyam — classical dance of Tamil Nadu; exponents include Rukmini Devi Arundale and Yamini Krishnamurthy.

• Kathakali — dance-drama of Kerala known for elaborate make-up (chutti) and costumes.

• Odissi — classical dance of Odisha; Kelucharan Mohapatra and Sonal Mansingh are famous exponents.

NOTE

• Kathak is the classical dance of Uttar Pradesh/North India; its gharanas are Lucknow, Jaipur and Banaras (and Raigarh).

• The eight classical dances: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam and Sattriya.

question: ब्रिता नृत्य (Brita Dance) किस राज्य का पारंपरिक लोकनृत्य है?
solution_text:
The correct answer is पश्चिम बंगाल (West Bengal).

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Brita (Vrita) dance is a traditional folk dance of West Bengal, performed by devotees — usually women — as a vow (vrata) after the fulfilment of a wish, such as recovery from a disease or the birth of a child. (व्रत नृत्य)

• It is a devotional/ritual dance offered in thanksgiving to the deity, and is also called Vrita or Brata dance.

• Other well-known folk dances of West Bengal are Chhau, Gambhira, Dhali, Jatra, Baul, Kathi and Domni.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Odisha (उड़ीसा) — folk dances include Chhau (Mayurbhanj), Ghumura, Ranapa, Dalkhai and Goti Pua.

• Rajasthan (राजस्थान) — Ghoomar, Kalbelia, Chari, Bhavai, Terah Taali and Kachhi Ghodi.

• Uttar Pradesh (उत्तरप्रदेश) — Raslila, Nautanki, Charkula, Jhora and Kajri.

NOTE

• Chhau dance (West Bengal, Odisha, Jharkhand) was inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2010, along with Kalbelia of Rajasthan.

• Baul songs of Bengal were inscribed by UNESCO in 2005/2008.

question: Which famous Indian dancer was given the title of Asthana Narthaki ("Resident Dancer") by the Tirumala Tirupathi Devasthanam temple, India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Yamini Krishnamurthy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Yamini Krishnamurthy (1940–2024) was conferred the title of 'Asthana Narthaki' (Resident Dancer) by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams in 1968. (आस्थान नर्तकी)

• She was a celebrated exponent of Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi and Odissi, and was trained at Kalakshetra under Rukmini Devi Arundale.

• She received the Padma Shri (1968), Padma Bhushan (2001) and Padma Vibhushan (2016), besides the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (1977).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Manjamma Jogati — a transgender folk artist of the Jogati Nritya of Karnataka, awarded the Padma Shri in 2021.

• Rukmini Devi Arundale — Bharatanatyam dancer who founded Kalakshetra (1936) in Chennai and revived Sadir as Bharatanatyam.

• Laxmi Narayan Tripathi — transgender rights activist and Bharatanatyam dancer.

NOTE

• Bharatanatyam greats: Balasaraswati, Rukmini Devi Arundale, Yamini Krishnamurthy, Padma Subrahmanyam, Mallika Sarabhai, Sonal Mansingh.

• Kuchipudi belongs to Andhra Pradesh; the Tirumala Venkateswara Temple at Tirupati is in Andhra Pradesh.

question: The microorganisms which convert the dead plants and animals to humus are known as ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is decomposers.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Decomposers are micro-organisms such as bacteria and fungi that break down dead plants and animals and convert them into humus, a dark organic matter in the soil. (अपघटक)

• They release nutrients back into the soil, making them available to plants, and thus complete the nutrient/biogeochemical cycle in an ecosystem.

• The process of converting organic waste into humus is called humification; decomposers are also called saprotrophs.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Producers — green plants and algae which prepare their own food by photosynthesis and form the first trophic level.

• Autotrophs — organisms that synthesise their own food from inorganic substances (same as producers).

• Herbivores — plant-eating animals (primary consumers) such as cow, goat and deer.

NOTE

• Food chain: Producers → Herbivores (primary consumers) → Carnivores (secondary/tertiary consumers) → Decomposers.

• Vermicomposting uses earthworms (Eisenia fetida) to convert organic waste into manure; the earthworm is called the 'farmer's friend'.

question: Mosquito belongs to _____ phylum of the animal kingdom.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Arthropoda.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Mosquito belongs to the phylum Arthropoda and the class Insecta; its order is Diptera (two-winged flies). (संधिपाद)

• Arthropods have a chitinous exoskeleton, jointed appendages, segmented body and an open circulatory system; it is the largest phylum of the animal kingdom.

• Examples: cockroach, butterfly, prawn, crab, scorpion, spider, centipede, housefly.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Ctenophora — 'sea walnuts' or 'comb jellies', marine animals with comb plates and bioluminescence.

• Chordata — animals with a notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord and pharyngeal gill slits; includes fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

• Mollusca — the second largest phylum, soft-bodied animals usually with a calcareous shell, e.g. snail, octopus, oyster, pila.

NOTE

• Mosquito-borne diseases: Malaria (female Anopheles), Dengue and Chikungunya (Aedes aegypti), Filariasis and Japanese Encephalitis (Culex).

• Only female mosquitoes bite, as they need blood protein for egg development.

question: निम्नलिखित में से किस स्थान पर अशोक के प्रमुख शिलालेख नहीं हैं?
solution_text:
The correct answer is साँची (Sanchi).

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sanchi (Madhya Pradesh) does not have a Major Rock Edict of Ashoka — it is famous for the Great Stupa (Stupa No. 1) and carries a Minor Pillar Edict (the Schism Edict). (साँची — प्रमुख शिलालेख नहीं)

• Ashoka's 14 Major Rock Edicts are found at sites such as Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat), Kalsi (Uttarakhand), Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra (Pakistan), Dhauli and Jaugada (Odisha), Sopara (Maharashtra) and Yerragudi (Andhra Pradesh).

• At Kandahar (Afghanistan) a bilingual Greek–Aramaic rock inscription of Ashoka was discovered.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Girnar rock also bears the later inscriptions of Rudradaman I (Junagadh inscription, first long Sanskrit inscription) and Skandagupta.

• Kalsi in Dehradun district is the only Major Rock Edict site in Uttarakhand.

• Ashokan inscriptions were first deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837.

NOTE

• The Sanchi Stupa was originally built by Ashoka and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1989).

• Scripts used in Ashokan edicts: Brahmi, Kharosthi, Greek and Aramaic; the Sarnath Lion Capital is India's State Emblem.

question: _____ was considered as the most important part of some of the earliest Hindu temples.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Garbhagriha.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Garbhagriha ('womb-house') is the small, usually cubical sanctum sanctorum where the main image of the deity is placed; it was the most important part of the earliest Hindu temples. (गर्भगृह)

• Only the priest was allowed to enter it, and rituals and worship were performed there.

• The earliest temples of the Gupta period (e.g. Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh and the temple at Sanchi, Temple No. 17) consisted mainly of a garbhagriha with a small porch.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Shikhara — the rising tower over the garbhagriha in Nagara style temples; in Dravida style the equivalent pyramidal tower is called Vimana.

• Mandapa — the pillared hall in front of the sanctum where devotees assemble.

• Other temple parts: Antarala (vestibule), Amalaka and Kalasha (crowning elements), Gopuram (gateway tower in South Indian temples).

NOTE

• Three main temple styles: Nagara (North India), Dravida (South India), Vesara (Deccan — a hybrid).

• Kailasa temple at Ellora (Rashtrakuta Krishna I) is a rock-cut Dravida temple; Brihadeeswara temple, Thanjavur was built by Rajaraja Chola I.

question: Who is the first Indian woman to have won a Grammy Award?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tanvi Shah.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Tanvi Shah became the first Indian woman to win a Grammy Award in 2010, for the song 'Jai Ho' from the film 'Slumdog Millionaire'. (पहली भारतीय महिला ग्रैमी विजेता)

• The award was in the category Best Song Written for a Motion Picture, Television or Other Visual Media, shared with A. R. Rahman and lyricist Gulzar; Tanvi Shah wrote and sang the Spanish lyrics.

• A. R. Rahman won two Grammys the same night (also Best Compilation Soundtrack) for the same film.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Asha Bhosle was nominated for a Grammy (1997, for 'Legacy' with Ali Akbar Khan) but did not win.

• Anuradha Paudwal and Alka Yagnik are noted Hindi playback singers and multiple Filmfare Award winners, but have not won a Grammy.

• Pandit Ravi Shankar was the first Indian to win a Grammy (1968).

NOTE

• Indian Grammy winners include Ravi Shankar, Zakir Hussain, Vishwa Mohan Bhatt, A. R. Rahman, Tanvi Shah, Ricky Kej, Falguni Shah (Falu) and Shankar Mahadevan (with Shakti, 2024).

• 'Jai Ho' also won the Academy Award (Oscar) for Best Original Song in 2009.

question: What is the national sport of Bhutan?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Archery.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Archery (Dha) is the national sport of Bhutan, declared so in 1971 when Bhutan joined the United Nations. (तीरंदाजी — भूटान)

• Archery competitions are held with great festivity in every village, accompanied by singing, dancing and traditional teasing of opponents.

• Bhutan's capital is Thimphu, currency Ngultrum, and it is famous for measuring progress through Gross National Happiness (GNH).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Ice Hockey is the national winter sport of Canada (lacrosse is its national summer sport).

• Cricket is popularly regarded as the national sport of Australia and England; India has no officially declared national game.

• Volleyball is the national sport of Sri Lanka.

NOTE

• Other national sports: Bangladesh — Kabaddi, Pakistan — Hockey, Nepal — Volleyball, Japan — Sumo wrestling, USA — Baseball, China — Table Tennis, Bhutan — Archery.

• Bhutan shares borders with India (Sikkim, West Bengal, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh) and China.

question: Which state became the first to implement "New Education Policy" at pre-primary level?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Uttarakhand.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Uttarakhand became the first state in India to implement the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 at the pre-primary level, launching it in 2022 in Anganwadi centres/Bal Vatikas. (उत्तराखंड — पहला राज्य)

• NEP 2020 was approved by the Union Cabinet on 29 July 2020, replacing the National Policy on Education, 1986.

• It introduced the 5+3+3+4 school structure in place of 10+2, covering children from age 3 onwards, and renamed the Ministry of Human Resource Development as the Ministry of Education.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Karnataka was the first state to issue orders to implement NEP 2020 at the higher-education level (2021).

• NEP 2020 was drafted by a committee headed by Dr. K. Kasturirangan, former ISRO chairman.

• The policy targets a GER of 50% in higher education by 2035 and public spending of 6% of GDP on education.

NOTE

• Uttarakhand was formed on 9 November 2000 as the 27th state; capital Dehradun (Gairsain is the summer capital).

• Earlier education commissions: University Education Commission (1948, Radhakrishnan), Secondary Education Commission (1952, Mudaliar), Kothari Commission (1964–66).

question: What is the relative charge of a proton and neutron?
solution_text:
The correct answer is +1 and 0 respectively.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A proton carries a relative charge of +1 (absolute charge +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb), while a neutron is electrically neutral, with a relative charge of 0. (प्रोटॉन धनावेशित, न्यूट्रॉन उदासीन)

• Protons and neutrons together are called nucleons and are present in the nucleus of an atom; the electron carries a relative charge of -1.

• Relative masses: proton ≈ 1 u, neutron ≈ 1 u, electron ≈ 1/1836 u (nearly negligible).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Electron was discovered by J. J. Thomson (1897); proton by E. Goldstein/Ernest Rutherford; neutron by James Chadwick (1932).

• Atomic number (Z) = number of protons; Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons.

• An atom is electrically neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons.

NOTE

• Isotopes — same atomic number, different mass number (e.g. ¹H, ²H, ³H); Isobars — same mass number, different atomic number (e.g. ⁴⁰Ar, ⁴⁰Ca).

• Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment (1911) established the existence of the small, dense, positively charged nucleus.

question:
Public goods possess which of the following features in the economy?

I. They are non-rivalrous.

II. They are non-excludable.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Public goods have two defining features — they are non-rivalrous and non-excludable. (सार्वजनिक वस्तुएँ)

• Non-rivalrous means one person's consumption does not reduce the amount available to others; non-excludable means no one can be prevented from using the good, even if they do not pay.

• Examples: national defence, street lighting, public parks, lighthouses, roads, public broadcasting and clean air.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Because of non-excludability, public goods suffer from the 'free rider' problem, so they are normally provided by the government rather than private markets.

• Private goods (e.g. food, clothes) are both rivalrous and excludable.

• Club goods are excludable but non-rivalrous (e.g. cable TV); common-pool resources are rivalrous but non-excludable (e.g. fisheries, grazing land).

NOTE

• Overuse of common resources is called the 'Tragedy of the Commons' (Garrett Hardin).

• Merit goods (education, healthcare) are under-consumed if left to the market, so the government subsidises them.

question: The months of ______ form a period of transition from hot rainy season to dry winter conditions.
solution_text:
The correct answer is October-November.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The months of October and November form the period of transition from the hot rainy season to dry winter conditions in India — this is the season of the retreating or north-east monsoon. (लौटता हुआ मानसून)

• With the apparent movement of the Sun southwards, the monsoon trough weakens and the low-pressure trough over north India is replaced by a high-pressure system, so the south-west monsoon withdraws.

• The oppressive weather of October, with high temperature and humidity, is popularly called 'October heat'.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Cyclones from the Bay of Bengal frequently strike the Coromandel Coast (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha) during October–December.

• Tamil Nadu gets most of its rainfall from this retreating (north-east) monsoon.

• September–October still falls largely within the withdrawing rainy season; December–January are the coldest winter months.

NOTE

• Four seasons of India: Cold Weather (December–February), Hot Weather (March–May), South-West Monsoon (June–September), Retreating Monsoon (October–November).

• The south-west monsoon normally arrives in Kerala around 1 June and withdraws completely by mid-December.

question: Which among the following is an international level professional auto racing sport?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Formula One.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Formula One (F1) is the highest class of international single-seater professional auto racing, governed by the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA). (कार रेसिंग)

• The FIA Formula One World Championship has been held since 1950; a season consists of a series of Grands Prix.

• India hosted the Indian Grand Prix at the Buddh International Circuit, Greater Noida, in 2011, 2012 and 2013.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Super Bowl — the championship game of the National Football League (NFL) in American football.

• Tour de France — the world's most famous cycling race, held annually in France; the leader wears the yellow jersey (maillot jaune).

• Wimbledon — the oldest tennis Grand Slam, played on grass courts in London.

NOTE

• Narain Karthikeyan was the first Indian F1 driver (2005); Karun Chandhok was the second.

• Terms in motor racing: Grand Prix, Pit stop, Pole position, Chicane, Formula, Lap.

• Michael Schumacher and Lewis Hamilton each hold a record seven F1 world titles.

question: Jhum cultivation or shifting cultivation is also known by the name of ________ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is Slash and burn agriculture.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Jhum/shifting cultivation is also called 'slash and burn' agriculture because farmers clear (slash) a patch of forest and burn the vegetation, then sow crops in the ash-enriched soil. (झूम खेती)

• After the fertility of the plot declines in two or three years, the land is abandoned and a new patch is cleared — it is a primitive subsistence form of farming.

• In India it is practised mainly in the North-Eastern states and is known by different local names: Jhum (Assam, North-East), Podu (Andhra Pradesh/Odisha), Bewar/Dahiya (Madhya Pradesh), Kumari (Western Ghats), Khil (Uttar Pradesh) and Penda (Chhattisgarh).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Plantation agriculture — a single cash crop (tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane) grown on a large estate with heavy capital and labour.

• Mixed farming — crop cultivation combined with livestock rearing on the same farm.

• Extensive farming — cultivation over large areas with low labour and capital input per hectare, common in the temperate grasslands.

NOTE

• International names for shifting cultivation: Milpa (Mexico/Central America), Ladang (Indonesia/Malaysia), Roca (Brazil), Ray (Vietnam), Chena (Sri Lanka), Masole (Congo).

• Shifting cultivation causes deforestation and soil erosion, hence it is discouraged.
